overview.text: A tokamak is an experimental device for studying controlled nuclear fusion. Its name comes from a Russian acronym meaning “toroidal chamber with magnetic coils.” Inside its doughnut-shaped chamber, fuel becomes plasma, a hot, electrically charged gas. Magnetic coils create fields that guide the plasma around the torus; combined, these fields twist and help confine it away from the chamber walls. Researchers use tokamaks to investigate conditions needed for fusion, but the machines are research devices, not commercial power stations. Developed through Soviet research in the late 1950s, the design’s first machine, T-1, began operating in Russia in 1958.

key_facts.text: A torus is the doughnut-like shape of a tokamak’s plasma chamber.
The toroidal magnetic field runs the long way around the torus; a poloidal field runs the short way around it.
Together, these magnetic fields form a twisted field that confines charged plasma particles.
The first tokamak, T-1, began operation in Russia in 1958.
ITER is designed to study fusion plasma; it is not designed to convert its fusion heat into electricity.
